subsection: 2. The main crises of the Cold War, Khrushchev and détente

notes.h: Background: the Cold War, the two alliances and the Soviet system
notes.b: The crises of 1958–62 and the détente that followed only make sense against a few basic facts: who the two sides were, how the Soviet state was run, and what nuclear weapons could do. The Cold War in Europe lasted from about 1945 to 1991.
points: The Cold War was a rivalry short of direct war between the USA and its Western allies (capitalist democracies) and the Soviet Union and its Eastern European satellites (communist one-party states). The superpowers never fought each other directly.
Instead the rivalry was fought through alliances, the arms race, propaganda, espionage, the space race and a series of crises, so each crisis was a test of nerve that stopped short of war.
The two sides formed alliances: NATO in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955. Germany was divided in 1949 into the Federal Republic (West) and the German Democratic Republic (East).

Berlin lay deep inside East Germany and was split into four sectors. The three Western sectors formed West Berlin, a Western island inside communist territory, which is why Berlin kept causing crises.

In the Soviet Union the Communist Party ruled alone. Its leader was the First Secretary of the Central Committee, the Presidium (later called the Politburo) was the inner leadership, and the chairman of the Council of Ministers (the premier) headed the government.

Stalin ruled by terror, purges (waves of arrests and executions), the Gulag labour camps and a cult of personality (public worship of the leader). His death on 5 March 1953 opened a struggle for the succession.

The USA used atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 and the Soviet Union tested its first in 1949. Both later built hydrogen bombs. Medium-range missiles reach targets within a region, while intercontinental missiles (ICBMs) reach the other superpower's homeland.
Fidel Castro took power in Cuba in January 1959 and Cuba then moved into the Soviet camp, which put a Soviet ally close to the USA.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask you to define terms such as the Cold War, and essays on the development of the Cold War want dates for each stage: origins from 1945, crises 1958–62, détente 1969–79, the second Cold War, then the end in 1985–91. This subsection supplies the middle stages.

notes.h: Early Cold War crises before 1953
notes.b: The crises before Khrushchev set the pattern of confrontation without direct war, and they explain why NATO was armed and why Germany stayed divided.
points: The Berlin Blockade (June 1948 to May 1949) was the first major crisis. It was ended by the Western airlift, and it confirmed the division of Germany. NATO was founded in 1949.
The Korean War began in June 1950 with the North Korean invasion of the South. It persuaded Western governments that communism was expansionist, so they rearmed.
As a result NATO was rearmed and given a unified command under Eisenhower, appointed its first Supreme Allied Commander in Europe in December 1950, and the West pushed to rearm West Germany.
Stalin's death on 5 March 1953 opened a more flexible phase, and an armistice in Korea followed in July 1953.

notes.h: Key personality: Nikita Khrushchev
notes.b: Khrushchev led the Soviet Union from Stalin's death in 1953 to 1964 and set the terms of the Cold War between de-Stalinisation and nuclear confrontation. He was shaped by Stalin's system, and then attacked it.
points: He was born in 1894 in Kalinovka, a village in Kursk province, of peasant stock. He worked as a miner and metalworker before rising through the Communist Party.
Under Stalin he became first secretary of the Moscow party organisation in 1935 and of the Ukrainian party in 1938, which shows he was a trusted servant of the Stalinist system.
He took part in Stalin's purges in Moscow and Ukraine in the late 1930s. This later made his attacks on Stalin's terror open to challenge, because he had helped to carry it out.

In the West contemporaries saw him as blustering, unpredictable and dangerous, but also as a man who could be dealt with, as shown by his 1959 visit to the USA and his 'kitchen debate' with Vice-President Nixon.
Mao Zedong's China called him a 'revisionist' who had betrayed Marxism-Leninism. By 1964 his Soviet colleagues saw him as a reckless leader of 'hare-brained schemes'.

Historians such as William Taubman, in Khrushchev: The Man and His Era (2003), describe a reformer who opened Soviet society after Stalin but whose policies were improvised and often failed, and who never built a lasting alternative to Stalinist planning.
notes.tip: In a 'how successful was Khrushchev' essay, state a verdict such as 'partly successful' at the start, argue it through paired points of success and failure, and end with his fall in 1964 as evidence.

notes.h: Key personality: Khrushchev's rise to power, 1953–58
notes.b: After Stalin's death no one had a clear right to rule, so Khrushchev won power by defeating rivals one at a time. Note that he held the party post first and became head of government only later.
points: He became First Secretary of the Central Committee in September 1953, the party post that was the real centre of power.
Lavrentiy Beria, the former secret police chief, was arrested in June 1953 and executed in December 1953, which removed the most feared rival.
Georgy Malenkov was forced to resign as premier in 1955, weakening another rival who had been the head of government since Stalin's death.
In June 1957 Khrushchev defeated the 'anti-party group' of Molotov, Malenkov and Kaganovich, with the help of Marshal Zhukov and the Central Committee.
In March 1958 he became chairman of the Council of Ministers (premier) as well as First Secretary, so from then on he held both the leading party post and the top government post.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level paragraphs on Khrushchev reward his rise in order, with dates and names: Beria, the anti-party group in 1957. Remember that he was First Secretary from 1953 but premier only from 1958.

notes.h: The secret speech and peaceful coexistence
notes.b: At the 20th Party Congress in 1956 Khrushchev did two things that changed Soviet politics: he attacked Stalin's record, and he redefined the Soviet struggle with the West as competition rather than war.
points: On 25 February 1956, in a secret speech to a closed session of the 20th Party Congress, he denounced Stalin's cult of personality and his terror against party members.
The attack was limited, because it condemned Stalin's crimes against party members and the cult of personality, not communism, collectivisation or the one-party state.
The text of the speech was published in the West in 1956, within months, so it soon became known across the world and not just in the Soviet bloc.
Its shock in Eastern Europe fed the Polish October of 1956, in which Władysław Gomułka came to power, and the Hungarian Uprising, because people hoped the bloc's rulers would loosen their control.
At the same congress he argued that war with the capitalist states was not inevitable. This became known as peaceful coexistence: competition would be economic and ideological, not military.
notes.tip: If asked to define peaceful coexistence, say that war with capitalism was not inevitable and the contest would be economic and ideological. In an essay, the speech unsettling the bloc and leading to Hungary is a cost to set against its benefits.

notes.h: De-Stalinisation in practice
notes.b: Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin was followed by real changes, which made Soviet life less frightening, though they stopped well short of democracy.
points: He released many political prisoners from the Gulag, the system of labour camps, so that people who had been held under Stalin returned to ordinary life.
The secret police were curbed, their role reduced, and they were placed under party control, so they could no longer act as a power above the party.
A cultural 'thaw' allowed more open discussion in literature, but it had limits, because the party still decided how far criticism could go.
At the 22nd Party Congress in October 1961 Stalin's body was removed from the Lenin Mausoleum, a public sign that his reputation had been cast down.
notes.tip: Use de-Stalinisation and the released prisoners as a success in a Khrushchev essay, and pair it with the cost that the speech unsettled the bloc.

notes.h: Farming and administration: the Virgin Lands and decentralisation
notes.b: Khrushchev tried to raise food output and make the economy more responsive. His schemes brought early gains but then failures, and the failures fed the resentment that ended his rule.
points: The Virgin Lands campaign from 1954 ploughed up grassland in Kazakhstan and western Siberia to grow grain, and it produced good harvests in its early years.
Soil erosion, drought and poor management later brought failures, most seriously in 1963, when the harvest was bad and grain had to be imported from the West.
After his 1959 visit to the USA he also launched a maize (corn) campaign, copying the American farms he had seen.
In 1957 industry was decentralised into regional economic councils (sovnarkhozy), so that decisions moved from Moscow ministries to the regions.
In 1962 the party was split into industrial and agricultural branches. Both reforms were resented by officials, because they threatened their jobs, and both were reversed by his successors.
notes.tip: Pair the Virgin Lands early harvests with the 1963 failure and grain imports, and do not forget that the repeated reorganisations angered the officials who later removed him.

notes.h: Living standards, promises and prestige
notes.b: Khrushchev promised Soviet citizens a better life and a race to overtake the USA. Space successes gave him prestige abroad, but the economy did not deliver at home.
points: He launched a large programme of new flats and promised more consumer goods, and he promised that the Soviet Union would overtake the USA.
The 1961 party programme at the 22nd Congress promised that communism would be built 'in the main' by 1980, a target that raised hopes that could not be met.
In June 1962 a strike at Novocherkassk over higher food prices and wage cuts was crushed when troops fired on the crowd and more than twenty people were killed, a sign of the limits of his reforms.
Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, was launched on 4 October 1957, and Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on 12 April 1961.
These successes alarmed the West, which feared a 'missile gap', meaning that the Soviet Union might be ahead in long-range missiles, and they boosted Soviet prestige.

notes.h: Foreign policy: the thaw of 1955 and its limits
notes.b: Peaceful coexistence showed in a series of gestures to the West and to Yugoslavia, but the limits of the policy showed when the Soviet bloc itself was challenged.
points: In May 1955 the Austrian State Treaty was signed: Soviet and Western troops left Austria and it became neutral, which showed Moscow could agree to a withdrawal.
In 1955 Khrushchev visited Josip Broz Tito in Belgrade to mend the split between the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia that had opened in 1948.
The Geneva summit of July 1955 brought together the USA, the USSR, Britain and France, and it was the first post-war summit of the four powers, so it signalled that talking was possible.
The Soviet crushing of the Hungarian Uprising in November 1956 showed that he would use force to keep the bloc together, whatever he said about coexistence.
In July 1959, at the American National Exhibition in Moscow, he and Vice-President Nixon held the 'kitchen debate' on the merits of communism and capitalism.
In September 1959 he visited the USA and held talks with President Eisenhower at Camp David, which produced the 'spirit of Camp David', a brief thaw that the U-2 incident later ended.
notes.tip: Examiners reward pairing peaceful coexistence and the Austrian treaty on the success side with Hungary on the failure side, which shows the limits of the policy.

notes.h: The Sino-Soviet split
notes.b: Khrushchev's changes divided the communist world. Mao's China rejected them, and the quarrel meant that Moscow could no longer speak for all communists.
points: Mao rejected de-Stalinisation and peaceful coexistence, regarding them as a betrayal of Marxism-Leninism. The ideological dispute grew from the late 1950s.
The dispute became open in 1960, when Soviet advisers were withdrawn from China, and open polemics (public attacks in print) followed in the early 1960s.
The split meant the Soviet Union faced two rival communist powers and could not count on Chinese support in Europe.
Albania sided with China, stopped taking part in the Warsaw Pact in the early 1960s and formally withdrew in 1968. The communist world was no longer united behind Moscow.
notes.tip: Remember that Albania formally left the Warsaw Pact in 1968 after taking no part for years, and that the split is one reason why détente later looked attractive to Moscow.

notes.h: Why Berlin mattered and the ultimatum of 1958
notes.b: Berlin was the most dangerous flashpoint in Europe, because West Berlin was an enclave inside East Germany and a window to the West. In 1958 Khrushchev tried to force the Western powers out.
points: West Berlin was a showcase of Western prosperity inside communist East Germany, so every East German could compare the two systems.
It was also the main escape route for East Germans. About 2.7 million people left East Germany for the West between 1949 and 1961 (sources vary slightly), mostly young and skilled.
This drained the GDR's workforce and threatened its survival, which is why Moscow and East Berlin wanted the exit closed.

On 27 November 1958 Khrushchev issued an ultimatum giving the Western powers six months to end their occupation of West Berlin and make it a demilitarised 'free city'. Otherwise he would hand control of access to East Germany.
The West refused and the deadline passed without Khrushchev carrying out his threat, so the ultimatum failed.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: the Berlin Blockade was 1948–49 and was Stalin's, the ultimatum was 1958, and the Wall was 1961. Remember the 2.7 million figure covers 1949 to 1961, not 1945.

notes.h: The U-2 incident and the Vienna summit
notes.b: After the thaw of 1959, two events in 1960 and 1961 ended hopes of a Berlin settlement and made a harder solution likely.
points: On 1 May 1960 an American U-2 spy plane flown by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union near Sverdlovsk.
Eisenhower would not apologise, so the Paris summit of May 1960 collapsed and the thaw of 1959 ended.
Powers was exchanged for a Soviet spy in February 1962, so the affair ended with a swap rather than a trial verdict standing.
At the Vienna summit in June 1961 Khrushchev pressed the new US president, John F. Kennedy (inaugurated January 1961), to accept a Berlin settlement.
Kennedy refused and strengthened US forces, so the crisis deepened over the summer.
notes.tip: Do not merge the two U-2 events: the plane shot down in 1960 wrecked the Paris summit, while a U-2 flight photographed the Cuban missiles in 1962.

notes.h: The Berlin Wall, 1961
notes.b: Faced with the refugee flow and a failed ultimatum, East Germany sealed the border. The Wall solved the GDR's problem but became the great symbol of a divided Europe.
points: East German forces under Walter Ulbricht began building the Berlin Wall overnight on 12–13 August 1961, with Soviet approval. At first it was barbed wire, then concrete, and it closed the border between the two halves of the city.
In October 1961 US and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie, but both sides drew back.
The Western powers protested but did not use force against the Wall. They accepted a divided city as better than war, which Khrushchev had judged correctly.
Between 1961 and 1989 the Wall and the border fortifications were guarded, and people who tried to cross were shot or arrested.
The refugee flow stopped and the GDR stabilised, and Soviet leaders regarded the Wall as a means of doing exactly that.
On 26 June 1963 Kennedy spoke in West Berlin and used the words 'Ich bin ein Berliner' to show Western support.
The Wall stood until 9 November 1989 and was the symbol of the divided Europe until then, because it showed that people had to be kept in by force.
notes.tip: Examiners like cause-and-result chains: refugee flow, then the Wall, then a stabilised GDR but a propaganda defeat for the East. Know the date of the Wall (13 August 1961) and its purpose.

notes.h: The Cuban Missile Crisis, 1962: motives and events
notes.b: The Cuban Missile Crisis was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear war, and it was resolved by a compromise.
points: Khrushchev wanted to protect Castro after the Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961, a failed US-backed invasion by Cuban exiles, not an invasion by American troops.

He also wanted to balance American Jupiter missiles in Turkey and Italy, and to make up for Soviet inferiority in long-range missiles, since medium-range missiles in Cuba could reach much of the USA. Possibly he also wanted leverage over Berlin.
Photographs from a U-2 flight of 14 October were shown to Kennedy on 16 October 1962 and revealed Soviet medium-range missiles being installed in Cuba.
Kennedy's advisers (ExComm, the Executive Committee of the National Security Council) weighed an air strike against a naval blockade and chose the blockade.
Kennedy announced a naval 'quarantine' of Cuba on 22 October 1962 and demanded the removal of the missiles. He avoided the word blockade because a blockade is an act of war.
For about a week the two superpowers were on the brink of war.
On 28 October 1962 Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba.
The secret part of the deal was a US promise to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey, which was done in 1963 and not made public at the time.
notes.tip: Remember the sequence: photographs on 16 October, quarantine on 22 October, settlement on 28 October 1962. The Jupiters in Turkey were a secret part of the deal.

notes.h: The Cuban Missile Crisis as seen from Europe, and its results
notes.b: For Europeans the crisis was a warning, because their fate seemed to be settled by the two superpowers while they looked on.
points: The European allies were informed, not consulted. Kennedy sent former secretary of state Dean Acheson to brief President de Gaulle in Paris, and de Gaulle gave firm support.
British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan was in regular contact with Kennedy during the crisis.
Europeans feared that the Soviets would answer a move on Cuba with a move on Berlin, so the crisis showed that Berlin and Cuba were linked.
The crisis made West European leaders more aware that decisions on nuclear war would be taken in Washington and Moscow, which strengthened de Gaulle's case for an independent French deterrent.
Khrushchev's prestige was damaged at home and in China, because the retreat looked like a defeat.
Both sides then sought safeguards: the Moscow–Washington hotline (1963) and the Partial Test Ban Treaty, signed on 5 August 1963.
notes.tip: A question on how the crises affected Europe wants consequences: the Wall, the hotline, French independence in defence and the peace movements. Cuba can be argued as the turning point that made both sides seek arms control.

notes.h: Nuclear deterrence and the arms race
notes.b: Each superpower relied on nuclear weapons to deter attack, and the arms race under Khrushchev made that deterrence ever more dangerous.
points: Nuclear deterrence means preventing attack by holding enough nuclear weapons to destroy an aggressor even after its first strike, a condition later called mutually assured destruction (MAD), a 1960s term.

In the mid-1950s the USA followed 'massive retaliation' (the threat of an all-out nuclear response, set out by John Foster Dulles in 1954). NATO shifted to 'flexible response', a range of possible responses, in 1967.
The Soviet Union tested the Tsar Bomba, about 50 megatons, on 30 October 1961, the largest nuclear explosion ever set off.
Western Europe depended on the US nuclear umbrella under NATO, yet there were doubts about whether the USA would risk its own cities to defend Europe.
Britain tested its first atomic bomb in 1952 and France in 1960, as part of an independent deterrent. France left NATO's integrated military command in 1966.
notes.tip: If asked to define nuclear deterrence, include the ability to destroy an aggressor after its first strike, and name MAD. In answers on Europe, link doubts about the US umbrella to France's independent deterrent.

notes.h: Arms control from 1963 to 1979
notes.b: The fear that deterrence could fail led to limited agreements. Each was a step, but none ended the arms race.
points: The Partial Test Ban Treaty, signed in Moscow on 5 August 1963 by the USA, Britain and the Soviet Union, banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water.
It did not ban underground tests, and France and China did not sign it, so its effect was limited.
The Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 is a different treaty: non-nuclear states promised not to acquire nuclear weapons, while the nuclear powers agreed to pursue disarmament.
SALT I was signed in Moscow on 26 May 1972 by Nixon and Brezhnev. It limited anti-ballistic missile systems (the ABM Treaty) and placed an interim limit on strategic missiles.
SALT II was signed in Vienna in June 1979 but was never ratified by the US Senate, and it was shelved after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the Test Ban Treaty (1963, atmosphere, space and water only) with the Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968). Cuba then the hotline and Test Ban Treaty is a standard cause-and-result chain.

notes.h: Détente: meaning and causes
notes.b: Détente means the easing of tension, from about 1969 to the late 1970s, through summits, arms-control treaties and treaties on European borders. It came about because both sides had reasons to want it.
points: Détente is usually dated from about 1969, with Nixon, Brezhnev and Brandt, and not from 1963. The hotline and Test Ban Treaty were its forerunners.
The shock of Cuba had shown both sides how close nuclear war could come, and the cost of the arms race was heavy.
By about 1970 the two sides had rough nuclear parity, so neither could expect to win an arms race.
The Soviet Union wanted Western trade and technology and recognition of the post-war borders.
The USA was entangled in Vietnam, and the Sino-Soviet split gave Moscow another reason to ease tension in the West.
West Germany wanted to ease the division of Germany.
notes.tip: Essays ask for the stages of the Cold War with dates, so give détente as 1969 to the late 1970s and name the causes for each side.

notes.h: Ostpolitik and the German settlement
notes.b: West Germany led the way in détente with Ostpolitik, a policy of reaching agreements with the East. It was Brandt's policy, not Adenauer's, and it settled many of the questions left by the war.
points: Willy Brandt, West German Chancellor from 1969 to 1974, pursued Ostpolitik to improve relations with Eastern Europe.
The Treaty of Moscow of 12 August 1970 renounced the use of force between the Federal Republic and the Soviet Union, so it removed a fear of war from the German question.

The Treaty of Warsaw of December 1970 recognised the Oder–Neisse line as Poland's western border, and Brandt knelt at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial, a gesture of remorse that won wide attention. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971.
The Four Power Agreement on Berlin of 3 September 1971 guaranteed access between West Berlin and West Germany and confirmed the Western presence in the city.
The Basic Treaty of December 1972 established relations between the Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic, which led to both joining the United Nations in 1973.
notes.tip: Keep the order straight: Moscow (August 1970), Warsaw (December 1970), the Four Power Agreement (September 1971), the Basic Treaty (December 1972). Remember Ostpolitik belongs to Brandt, not Adenauer.

notes.h: The Helsinki Final Act, 1975
notes.b: The Helsinki conference was the high point of détente. It gave each side something it wanted, and over time the Western gain proved the more important.
points: The Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe produced the Helsinki Final Act on 1 August 1975, signed by 35 states including the USA, Canada and the Soviet Union.
It treated the post-war borders in Europe as inviolable, a Soviet gain, because Moscow had long wanted its control of Eastern Europe accepted.
It committed the signatories to respect human rights, a Western gain, and later Eastern dissidents used this commitment to press their governments.
It was not a peace treaty and was not legally binding, so it relied on the signatories' political commitment.
notes.tip: Learn the pairing: borders as a Soviet gain, human rights as a Western gain. Helsinki is a favourite example of détente's achievements.

notes.h: Afghanistan and the end of détente
notes.b: Détente broke down in the late 1970s. Its end opened the second Cold War, a phase of renewed confrontation.
points: Soviet forces invaded Afghanistan in December 1979, which ended détente because it convinced the USA that Moscow was expansionist again.
The USA responded with a grain embargo in January 1980 and, with some allies, a boycott of the Moscow Olympics in 1980.
SALT II, signed in June 1979, was shelved and never ratified by the US Senate, so the arms limits it would have set never took effect.
Détente had collapsed because each side read it differently and the arms building had continued.

notes.h: The Euromissiles and the peace movement
notes.b: A new arms race in Europe led to the deployment of intermediate-range missiles in the early 1980s, and it provoked mass protest.
points: The Soviet Union deployed SS-20 intermediate-range missiles aimed at Western Europe from the late 1970s, which threatened Western European cities.
NATO's double-track decision of 12 December 1979 agreed to deploy Pershing II and ground-launched cruise missiles unless talks with the Soviet Union succeeded.
The talks failed. Deployment began in November 1983 and the Soviet delegation walked out of the Geneva arms talks that month.
Large peace demonstrations took place in West Germany, Britain and the Netherlands in 1981–83 against the new missiles.
One example was the Greenham Common women's peace camp in Berkshire, England, which began in 1981.
notes.tip: The Euromissile crisis was not defused by talks: they broke down in 1983 and the missiles were deployed. They were removed only by the INF Treaty of 1987 under Gorbachev.

notes.h: Reagan's hard line and the way out
notes.b: Ronald Reagan's election brought a harder line towards Moscow. This raised tension to its highest point since Cuba before talks reversed it.
points: Reagan was elected in November 1980. In March 1983 he called the Soviet Union an 'evil empire', and he announced the Strategic Defense Initiative ('Star Wars') in the same month.
In November 1983 NATO held the exercise Able Archer 83. Soviet fears of a surprise attack were heightened, though historians still debate how alarmed Soviet leaders really were.
Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985, which opened a new phase because he was willing to negotiate real cuts.
At the Reykjavik summit in October 1986 the two leaders discussed deep cuts in weapons.
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty was signed in Washington in December 1987 and removed the Euromissiles.

notes.h: The turning points of the Cold War to 1989
notes.b: Examiners ask which events changed the course of the Cold War, so know the order and what each one changed.
points: Berlin Blockade, 1948–49: confirmed the division of Germany and led to NATO.
Stalin's death in 1953 began a more flexible phase, and the Korean armistice followed in July 1953.
Hungary, November 1956: the crushing of the uprising showed that the Soviet Union would use force to keep its bloc together.
Berlin Wall (1961) and Cuba (1962) were the high points of confrontation, after which both sides sought safeguards such as the hotline and the Test Ban Treaty.

Prague Spring: Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968, confirming the Brezhnev Doctrine, the Soviet claim that it could intervene to keep communism in power in the bloc, but it did not end détente.
Helsinki, 1975: the high point of détente, which gave dissidents in the East a human rights standard.
Afghanistan and the double-track decision, 1979, ended détente and began the second Cold War, and Reagan's election in 1980 hardened it.

Gorbachev from 1985, the Reykjavik summit of October 1986 and the INF Treaty of 1987 reversed the arms race, and 1989 ended Soviet control of eastern Europe (see the notes on reform movements and the collapse of communism).
notes.tip: Choose a few turning points, put them in order and argue what each changed: hardened division, eased tension, began détente or ended it. Credit goes to judgement, for example Cuba as the turning point that made both sides seek arms control.

notes.h: Key personality: Khrushchev's fall, 1964
notes.b: Khrushchev's removal showed that the party, not the leader, held the final power. It was also unusual, because he was not killed or imprisoned.
points: On 14 October 1964 the Central Committee removed him from the posts of First Secretary and chairman of the Council of Ministers. He had been on holiday on the Black Sea coast and was recalled.
Leonid Brezhnev became First Secretary and Alexei Kosygin became chairman of the Council of Ministers, so the two posts were again held by different men.
His critics cited the Cuban retreat, the failing agriculture, the repeated reorganisations that angered party officials, and his erratic personal style.
He was pensioned off and lived in retirement, largely at a dacha (country house) outside Moscow, until his death in 1971. He was the first Soviet leader removed without being killed or imprisoned.
His fall confirmed that the Soviet leadership would not tolerate a single figure dominating policy, which shaped the more collective style of the Brezhnev years.
notes.tip: Give the date, 14 October 1964, and the reasons in order, and end a Khrushchev essay with his fall as evidence of his failures. Do not reverse the roles of Brezhnev (First Secretary) and Kosygin (premier).

notes.h: Assessment: détente's achievements and limits
notes.b: Détente is judged by what it achieved in treaties and what it failed to change in the arms race.
points: Achievements: arms limits in SALT I, the German treaties such as the Moscow Treaty and the Basic Treaty, and Helsinki's human rights standard.
Limits: arms building continued despite the agreements, and each side read détente differently, since the West hoped for restraint and the Soviet Union for recognition of its gains.
Détente ended in 1979 with Afghanistan and the Euromissiles, which suggests it had never settled the basic rivalry.
notes.tip: Examiners reward paired points with dates, such as arms limits and the German treaties against continued arms building and collapse in 1979.

notes.h: Assessment: Khrushchev's achievements and failures
notes.b: Khrushchev's record is judged by contrasting his bold moves with the setbacks that ended his rule, and a stated verdict such as 'partly successful' scores better than a narrative.
points: At home, his achievements were de-Stalinisation, the release of prisoners, the housing programme and the space successes of Sputnik and Gagarin.
At home, his failures were the Virgin Lands crisis, the reversed reorganisations, Novocherkassk and promises that went unkept.
Abroad, his achievements were peaceful coexistence, the Austrian State Treaty, the hotline and the Test Ban Treaty.
Abroad, his failures were Hungary, the failed Berlin ultimatum, the Wall (a propaganda defeat), the Cuban retreat and the split with China.
Compared with Gorbachev: both were reformers from above who lost power. Khrushchev kept the one-party system and the bloc by force, while Gorbachev let both go.
Contemporary Western views often saw a bully and gambler, and his Soviet colleagues attacked a schemer whose 'hare-brained schemes' and boasting were reckless.
Later historians judge him as a reformer who made the system less brutal and opened it, but never built a lasting alternative to Stalinist planning.
notes.tip: A comparison essay with Gorbachev needs parallel points: both reformed from above, both met resistance and both lost power. For Khrushchev, argue through pairs: de-Stalinisation against Hungary, Virgin Lands against 1963, coexistence against the Wall and Cuba.

keyTerms.definition: The strategy of preventing attack by possessing nuclear weapons able to inflict unacceptable damage on an aggressor after a first strike.
The easing of Cold War tension from about 1969, marked by arms control agreements and improved contact between East and West.
The rivalry from 1945 to 1991 between the USA and its allies and the Soviet Union and its eastern European bloc, short of direct war between them.
Khrushchev's policy after 1956 of condemning Stalin's terror and personality cult, and loosening political controls.
The Soviet doctrine announced in 1956 that the communist and capitalist systems could compete without war between them.
West German chancellor Willy Brandt's policy of normalising relations with the Soviet Union and eastern European states, begun around 1969.
The condition in which each superpower could destroy the other with nuclear weapons even after absorbing a first strike, which discouraged war.
The 1963 agreement by the USA, Britain and the Soviet Union banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water.
Khrushchev's programme from 1954 to plough up grassland in Kazakhstan and Siberia to grow grain.
The fortified barrier built by East Germany from 13 August 1961 to stop people leaving East Berlin for the West.
The 1975 agreement of 35 states that recognised Europe's post-war borders and pledged respect for human rights.
The Soviet SS-20 and the NATO Pershing II and cruise missiles of the late 1970s and 1980s, whose deployment caused the missile crisis in Europe.

factCards.definition: Khrushchev denounced Stalin to a closed session of the 20th Party Congress on 25 February 1956.
On 27 November 1958 Khrushchev demanded a settlement within six months that would end the Western occupation of West Berlin.
Francis Gary Powers' spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union on 1 May 1960, wrecking the Paris summit.

factCards.term: Berlin Wall: first day of construction
factCards.definition: East German forces began sealing the border between East and West Berlin on 13 August 1961.
President Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of Cuba on 22 October 1962.
On 28 October 1962 Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles from Cuba in return for a US pledge not to invade.
Signed in Moscow on 5 August 1963 by the USA, Britain and the Soviet Union.

factCards.term: Why Khrushchev placed missiles in Cuba
factCards.definition: To defend Castro after the Bay of Pigs, to offset American missiles in Turkey and Italy, and to make up for Soviet weakness in long-range missiles.
